commonErrors.example: A learner writes on the worksheet that sound travels faster than light, picking the statement that the thunder reaches us first because it is so loud.

fixIt.corrected: Corrected working: light is far faster than sound, so the lightning flash arrives first and the thunder follows seconds later.
fixIt.prompt: Fix it: say which arrives first from a distant strike and give the two speeds that settle it.

commonErrors.example: On the exit ticket, a learner answers that the thunder is noticed first from a distant storm instead of the lightning flash.

fixIt.corrected: Corrected check: the flash travels at about 300,000,000 m/s and arrives almost instantly, while the thunder travels at only 340 m/s - the flash is first.
fixIt.prompt: Fix it: give the one-sentence correction for the claim that sound travels faster than light.

modelAnswers.answer: The particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel, bunching together and spreading apart in turn. The particles stay in place overall; the wave carries energy from place to place.
modelAnswers.question: Describe how the particles move in a longitudinal sound wave, and state what the wave itself carries.
A sound wave travels at 340 m/s with frequency 170 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.

nextSteps: Reteach the trap with the storm sequence, landing that light is far faster than sound and the flash always arrives before the thunder.
Practise the check from the teacher script - rearrange before substituting: wavelength = v / f, then verify with 170 Hz x 2 m = 340 m/s.
strengths: Most of the class can rearrange the wave equation to find a wavelength, such as reading 340 metres per second at 170 hertz on the worksheet as a wavelength of 2 metres.
The class can describe longitudinal particle motion - bunching and spreading along the direction of travel - and can state that the wave carries energy.
subject: science
title: Waves: light, sound and the wave equation
